# Dalton's atomic theory and its postulates

## 1. Topic Introduction
Dalton's atomic theory, proposed by John Dalton in 1803–1808 and published in *A New System of Chemical Philosophy* (1808), was the first quantitative theory of matter. It explained the experimentally established laws of chemical combination — conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions — by assuming that matter is made of discrete, indestructible particles called atoms. The theory marks the birth of modern chemistry because it converted qualitative ideas about matter into a testable, quantitative model that underlies all stoichiometric calculation.

Why it matters: every mole calculation, balanced equation and limiting-reactant problem in this unit rests on Dalton's two surviving ideas — matter is atomic, and chemical reactions only rearrange atoms.

What you will learn: the six postulates in order; how each law of chemical combination follows from them; the successes that made the theory accepted; the limitations revealed by electrons, protons, neutrons, isotopes, isobars and nuclear reactions.

Learning outcomes: state the six postulates; link each postulate to a law of chemical combination; discuss at least three limitations with examples; solve a law-of-multiple-proportions numerical showing a simple whole-number ratio.

## 2. Fundamental Conceptual Understanding
**What it is:** Dalton's atomic theory is a model of matter in which every element is composed of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms, and a chemical reaction is a rearrangement of these atoms rather than a creation or destruction of matter.

**Why it exists:** Before Dalton, chemists knew that elements combine in fixed proportions (definite proportions) and that two elements can form several compounds (multiple proportions), but no one had a particle model that explained *why*. Dalton's atoms gave a mechanical reason: fixed atom counts in a formula unit give fixed mass ratios; whole-number atom combinations give whole-number mass ratios.

**How it works:** Each postulate makes an idealised claim about atoms. Together they let chemists (i) balance equations by atom conservation, (ii) assign relative atomic masses, and (iii) predict the formulas of compounds from combining ratios — the entire quantitative basis of stoichiometry.

**Components:** atoms (of each element), elements (identical atoms), compounds (atoms of different elements in fixed ratios), chemical reactions (rearrangements only).

**Interactions:** atoms of different elements combine in fixed simple whole-number ratios to form compounds; in a reaction the same atoms that entered leave, merely recombined.

**Importance:** It is the foundation of the mole concept, relative atomic mass, formula determination and all of quantitative chemistry.

## 3. Scientific Definitions

| Term | Scientific meaning | Explanation | Importance |
|------|-------------------|-------------|-------------|
| Atom | The smallest particle of an element that can take part in a chemical reaction | Dalton treated it as indivisible and indestructible; modern view: divisible into subatomic particles | Central unit of the theory; basis of atomic mass |
| Element | A substance made of only one kind of atom | Atoms of the same element are identical in mass and properties in Dalton's model | Defines chemical identity |
| Compound | A substance formed when atoms of different elements combine in a fixed simple whole-number ratio | Fixed atom count in the formula unit gives a fixed mass ratio (law of definite proportions) | Explains why compounds have fixed composition |
| Chemical reaction | A process in which atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed | The atoms in the products are exactly the atoms in the reactants | Basis of the law of conservation of mass and of balanced equations |
| Law of conservation of mass | Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products in a chemical reaction | Follows because atoms are merely rearranged | Reason every equation must be balanced |
| Law of definite proportions | A given compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed proportion by mass | A fixed formula means a fixed atom count and hence a fixed mass ratio | Enables percentage-composition calculations |
| Law of multiple proportions | When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in small whole-number ratios | Whole atoms combine in whole-number ratios (e.g. CO vs CO₂) | Strongest evidence for the atomic theory |

**Keywords:** atom, element, compound, chemical reaction, postulate, indivisible, whole-number ratio, conservation of mass, definite proportions, multiple proportions.

## 4. Detailed Explanation
Dalton's six postulates (stated in the order Dalton gave them):

1. **Matter is composed of extremely small, indivisible particles called atoms.** Atoms cannot be subdivided by chemical means.
2. **All atoms of a given element are identical in mass, size and chemical properties; atoms of different elements differ in mass and properties.** This is why each element has a characteristic relative atomic mass.
3. **Atoms are neither created nor destroyed nor divided in a chemical reaction.** A chemical change only rearranges atoms — this explains conservation of mass.
4. **Atoms of different elements combine in fixed, simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.** A compound has a fixed formula (e.g. H₂O is always 2 H : 1 O), which explains definite proportions.
5. **The atom is the smallest particle that can take part in a chemical reaction.** Molecules, where they exist, are built from atoms held by chemical attraction.
6. **Atoms of one element cannot be changed into atoms of another element by ordinary chemical means.** (Nuclear reactions later showed this is false.)

**Successes (why it was accepted):** explained conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions by pure logic; provided the basis for balancing equations and hence all stoichiometry; introduced relative atomic masses; prepared the ground for the mole concept and Avogadro's molecular hypothesis.

**Limitations and modifications:**
1. Atoms are divisible — discovery of the electron (Thomson, 1897), proton (Rutherford, 1919) and neutron (Chadwick, 1932) showed atoms contain subatomic particles.
2. Not all atoms of an element are identical — isotopes (¹²C, ¹³C, ¹⁴C; ³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl) have the same chemistry but different masses.
3. Atoms of different elements can have the same mass — isobars such as ⁴⁰Ar and ⁴⁰Ca.
4. Atoms of one element can be changed into another — nuclear reactions/transmutation (¹⁴N + α → ¹⁷O + p; radioactivity, fission, fusion).
5. Mass is not strictly conserved in nuclear processes — mass defect appears as energy (E = mc²); conservation of mass holds only for ordinary chemical reactions.
6. It did not explain chemical bonding, atomic structure, gaseous volumes, reciprocal proportions, allotropes or diatomic element molecules until Avogadro's molecular concept.

**Summing up:** Dalton's core idea — matter is atomic and reactions only rearrange atoms — remains valid; his absolute claims about indivisibility, identical masses and non-convertibility are the parts modern chemistry modified.

## 5. Biological Examples

| Example | Classification | Distinguishing characteristics | Why it belongs | Importance |
|---------|---------------|-------------------------------|----------------|-------------|
| Urea (CO(NH₂)₂) fertiliser | Compound | Fixed atom ratio 1 C : 1 O : 2 N : 4 H; fixed mass ratio C:O:N:H = 12:16:28:8 = 3:4:7:2 | Manufactured in Nepal for agriculture; its composition never varies, illustrating definite proportions | Shows how fixed composition underpins fertiliser dosing and trade |
| Cement (calcium silicates/aluminates) | Compound mixture | Fixed formulas in each phase (e.g. Ca₃SiO₅); reactions conserve atoms during setting | Local construction material; setting is atom rearrangement | Links stoichiometry to building materials and quality control |
| Fermentation (glucose → ethanol + CO₂) | Chemical reaction | C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂; atoms conserved, rearranged | Traditional food/beverage process; illustrates conservation of mass in a familiar context | Connects atomic rearrangement to observable mass balance

## 6. Chemical Processes and Mechanisms
Chemical change as rearrangement of atoms — numbered account:
1. **Definition:** A chemical reaction is a process in which bonds break and form such that the atoms present before the reaction are the same atoms present after, merely regrouped.
2. **Location:** Occurs at the particle scale during collisions of reacting particles; observable at the macro scale as colour change, precipitate, gas evolution or temperature change.
3. **Requirements:** Reactant particles must collide with sufficient energy and proper orientation; atoms must be present in the combining ratios fixed by the compound formulas.
4. **Components:** Reactant atoms, product atoms, and the balanced equation that records the rearrangement.
5. **Sequential steps:** (i) Write correct formulas of reactants and products. (ii) Balance the equation so atom counts match on both sides (conservation of atoms). (iii) Use coefficients as mole ratios for calculation.
6. **Result:** No atom is created or destroyed; total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.
7. **Significance:** This atom-rearrangement picture is why stoichiometric calculations (mass–moles–mass, limiting reactant, yield) are valid and why equations must be balanced before any calculation.

## 8. Conceptual Relationships
**Within topic:** The six postulates form a chain — indivisible atoms → identical atoms of an element → atoms rearranged, not created → fixed combining ratios → atom as reaction participant → elements not interconverted chemically. Each postulate supports one or more laws of chemical combination.
**To other units:** Relative atomic mass (structure of atom unit), mole concept and Avogadro's number (later in this unit), chemical bonding (later units), nuclear chemistry (mass–energy, transmutation).
**To real life:** Fertiliser formulation (urea), cement setting, combustion, analytical gravimetry — all depend on fixed composition and atom conservation.

## 9. Important Facts and Scientific Terminology

| Term | Scientific meaning | Explanation | Importance |
|------|-------------------|-------------|-------------|
| Relative atomic mass | Mass of an atom relative to 1/12 of a ¹²C atom | Introduced by Dalton; basis of the atomic mass scale | Converts atom counts to weighable masses |
| Isotope | Atoms of the same element with different masses (e.g. ³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl) | Disproves Dalton's 'identical atoms' postulate | Average atomic mass reflects natural isotopic mix |
| Isobar | Atoms of different elements with the same mass number (e.g. ⁴⁰Ar, ⁴⁰Ca) | Same mass number, different atomic number | Shows mass alone does not identify an element |
| Mass defect | Difference between nuclear mass and sum of nucleon masses | Appears as energy (E = mc²) | Shows mass is not strictly conserved in nuclear change |
| Transmutation | Conversion of one element into another | Occurs in nuclear reactions | Disproves Dalton's 'elements not interconverted' postulate |
| Avogadro number | N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ | Links mole to particle count | Connects Dalton's atomic idea to measurable quantities |

## 10. Topic Mastery Check

### Important definitions
1. Atom — smallest particle of an element that takes part in a chemical reaction.
2. Element — substance made of one kind of atom.
3. Compound — atoms of different elements in a fixed simple whole-number ratio.
4. Law of conservation of mass — total reactant mass equals total product mass.
5. Law of definite proportions — a pure compound has fixed elemental proportions by mass.
6. Law of multiple proportions — masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of another are in simple whole-number ratios.

### Key concepts to remember
- Matter is atomic; chemical reactions only rearrange atoms.
- Fixed formula ⇒ fixed mass ratio (definite proportions).
- Whole-number atom combinations ⇒ whole-number mass ratios (multiple proportions).
- Conservation of mass is why equations must be balanced.

### Important classifications
- Postulates later modified: indivisibility (subatomic particles), identical masses (isotopes), non-convertibility (nuclear reactions), strict mass conservation (nuclear mass defect).
- Postulates still valid: atoms exist; reactions rearrange atoms.

### Important comparisons
| Dalton's claim | Modern status | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Atoms indivisible | Modified | Electron, proton, neutron exist |
| Atoms of an element identical | Modified | Isotopes ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl |
| Elements not interconverted | Modified | Nuclear transmutation ¹⁴N + α → ¹⁷O + p |
| Mass strictly conserved | Modified for nuclear only | Mass defect → E = mc² |

### Common conceptual confusions
- Dalton's theory is not 'completely wrong' — its core (matter is atomic; reactions rearrange atoms) is valid; only its absolute claims were modified.
- Dalton did not explain the law of gaseous volumes — that was Gay-Lussac; Avogadro's hypothesis was needed to interpret it.
- Nuclear reactions violate Dalton's postulates; they are outside ordinary chemical stoichiometry.

### Short-answer questions
1. State any two postulates of Dalton's atomic theory. (2 marks)
2. Which law of chemical combination is directly explained by Dalton's theory? (1 mark)
3. How does Dalton's theory explain the law of conservation of mass? (2 marks)

### Long-answer questions
1. State the six postulates of Dalton's atomic theory and discuss its limitations in light of modern discoveries. (8 marks)
2. Explain how Dalton's atomic theory accounts for the laws of conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions. (5 marks)

### Conceptual questions
1. Which postulate is contradicted by (a) isotopes, (b) isobars, (c) nuclear reactions? Explain each. (3 marks)
2. Is Dalton's atomic theory completely wrong today? Justify. (2 marks)

### Application-based questions
1. Carbon forms CO and CO₂. Show that the data obey the law of multiple proportions. (3 marks)
2. A sealed tube containing AgNO₃ and NaCl solutions is mixed; why does its mass remain constant? (2 marks)

### Answers
1. (a) Matter is composed of indivisible atoms. (b) Atoms of the same element are identical; atoms of different elements differ. (any two postulates, 1 mark each)
2. Law of multiple proportions.
3. Atoms are only rearranged, not created or destroyed, so total mass is unchanged.
4. Long answer 1: six postulates (1 mark each) + limitations: isotopes, isobars, subatomic particles, nuclear transmutation, mass–energy (2 marks). Long answer 2: link postulate 3 to conservation, postulate 4 to definite proportions, postulate 4 whole-number ratios to multiple proportions (1 mark each link).
5. Conceptual: (a) isotopes contradict identical masses; (b) isobars (⁴⁰Ar/⁴⁰Ca) contradict 'different elements have different masses'; (c) nuclear reactions contradict non-convertibility and mass conservation.
6. Application 1: fixed 12 g C combines with 16 g O (CO) and 32 g O (CO₂); ratio 16:32 = 1:2, a simple whole-number ratio. Application 2: atoms only rearranged into AgCl and NaNO₃, so total mass is unchanged — conservation of mass.

### PYQ Solutions
**2079:** Postulate: matter is made of indivisible atoms — limitation: atoms are divisible (electron/proton/neutron exist). Postulate: atoms of the same element are identical in mass — limitation: isotopes (³⁵Cl, ³⁷Cl) differ in mass. (1 mark postulate + 1 mark limitation each.)
**2078:** Law of multiple proportions.
**2077:** Limitations: atoms divisible (subatomic particles); not all atoms of an element identical (isotopes); atoms of different elements can have same mass (isobars); elements interconvertible in nuclear reactions; mass not strictly conserved in nuclear change (E = mc²); did not explain bonding/gaseous volumes. Award 1 mark per valid limitation, up to 5.
**2076:** Atoms are neither created nor destroyed, only rearranged, so total mass of reactants equals total mass of products.
**2075:** In CO, 12 g C combines with 16 g O; in CO₂, 12 g C combines with 32 g O. For fixed carbon, oxygen masses are 16:32 = 1:2 — a simple whole-number ratio, obeying multiple proportions.

*Note: PYQ years 2075–2079 are representative NEB-style questions; verify against official NEB papers where available.*

## 12. Summary and Self-check
Dalton's atomic theory (1808) proposed that matter is made of indivisible atoms, that atoms of an element are identical, that atoms are rearranged (not created/destroyed) in reactions, and that atoms combine in fixed simple whole-number ratios. These postulates explain conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions and underpin all stoichiometry. Modern discoveries modified the absolute claims: atoms are divisible (subatomic particles), isotopes exist (not all atoms of an element identical), isobars exist, nuclear reactions interconvert elements, and mass–energy equivalence means mass is not strictly conserved in nuclear change. The core idea — matter is atomic and reactions only rearrange atoms — remains valid.

Self-check: Can you state all six postulates in order? Link each to a law? Name three limitations with examples? Solve CO vs CO₂ for multiple proportions? If yes, you have mastered this topic.
